title: Transparency Theater + Misaligned Incentives: When More Documentation Means Less Safety

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: directly tests whether governance standards requiring documentation volume create compliance without safety. A decoupled finding would be an actionable critique of current governance design.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: rubric-based coding of documents for specificity, testability, and actionability is accessible. CS students can apply a well-defined rubric to safety reports with moderate training.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: sample of AI safety reports, count quantity metrics, apply quality rubric, compute correlation. Clear methodology with bounded inputs and outputs.

novelty.reasoning: The concept of transparency without genuine safety is discussed in several sources. 'The Explainability Illusion: Why AI Transparency Requirements Miss the Point' (National Law Review, 2025) argues organizations create the appearance of transparency without understanding. 'A Trustworthy AI Reality-Check: The Lack of Transparency of AI Products in Healthcare' (Frontiers in Digital Health, 2024) found major documentation gaps in ethical considerations and safety monitoring. Medium's 'Why Most AI Safety Policies Fail in Practice' (2026) addresses compliance without actual safety. However, the specific empirical approach of sampling AI safety reports and correlating documentation volume metrics with quality rubric scores (specificity, testability, actionability) to test whether quantity is decoupled from quality has not been done. This quantitative test of the hypothesis is a novel contribution.

evidence: The Explainability Illusion: Why AI Transparency Requirements Miss the Point. National Law Review, 2025.
